deeper.title: What the price assumes
deeper.text: The price assumes about 22% a year growth in free cash flow for 10 years, then 3% (discount rate 10.0% = 10-year Treasury 5.0% + 5%; base: last 12 months of free cash flow). For comparison, sales grew 18% last year; 17%/yr over 3 years — roughly in line with its recent growth.

deeper.title: Return on capital
deeper.text: 30% (3 years ago 51%, falling) — each $100 invested in the business (debt + equity, net of cash) earns about $30 a year after tax; return on shareholders' equity 30% (3 years ago 35%).

deeper.title: Signed future revenue
deeper.text: Signed but not yet delivered (remaining performance obligations): $683.0B, up 72% from a year ago — about 2.0× the last 12 months of sales; customer prepayments not yet earned (deferred revenue): $69.6B, up 13% from a year ago.

deeper.title: Multi-year view
deeper.text: Sales grew 17%/yr over 3 years and 14%/yr over 5 years; operating margin today 47% vs a 5-year range of 41–47% (median 45%): near the top of a fairly narrow range.
deeper.margin_position: near the top of a fairly narrow range

deeper.title: Cash returned to shareholders
deeper.text: Returned $48.0B to shareholders over the last 12 months ($21.0B buybacks + $27.0B dividends) = 1.3% of the company's market value. Share count down 0.3% from a year ago (about flat).

deeper.title: Analyst estimates
deeper.text: Next year's earnings-per-share estimate $24.20, up 3% in 90 days (up 2% in the last 30); 25 analysts raised, 3 cut in 30 days. This year's earnings-per-share estimate $20.01, up 1% in 90 days (up 1% in the last 30); 25 analysts raised, 3 cut in 30 days. Source: Yahoo (unofficial).

deeper.title: Vs peers

deeper.title: Where sales come from
deeper.text: By segment, latest quarter vs a year earlier: Agents and infra 83% of sales, up 25%; Devices and consumer 17% of sales, down 3%. Source: 10-Q XBRL.

deeper.title: Insider trading
deeper.text: Last 90 days: no open-market purchases; sales $74.8M, 96% under pre-set 10b5-1 trading plans. Source: SEC Form 4.

summary.thesis: The business keeps getting better, but free cash flow fell from 78.0B to 60.0B, so the price only makes sense if heavy spending starts paying back.
summary.decision: Hold. Add only near the low end of the stock's usual valuation range, and leave the swing trade alone until price picks a side.

note.happening: Microsoft fell 2.77% to 484.52. It closed below the 486.0–491.22 zone, which had 8 touches and was yesterday's add level. That zone now sits overhead as resistance, a price area where selling has capped rallies. There is no news since the last note, and the next earnings report is on 2027-01-27.
note.business: Today's drop is about price, not the business. There is no news, so nothing about demand, margins or competition changed today. The latest filed quarter is still solid. Sales grew 18.8% from a year earlier, up from 18.3% two quarters ago. The operating margin (the share of sales left after running costs) rose to 47.1% from 46.27%. The balance sheet has 29.0B more cash than debt, and the share count shrank 0.27%. Analysts keep raising their numbers. The next-year earnings-per-share estimate rose to 24.2 from 23.68 thirty days ago. Cash is the weak spot. Free cash flow, the cash left after investment, fell to 60.0B from 78.0B, and only 17.31% of sales turns into free cash. The filings say each dollar invested now earns 30¢ a year, down from 51¢ three years ago. The spending is real, but it is not paying back yet (general knowledge: much of it is reported to be AI data-center build-out). Earnings power is not at risk. The risk is that cash returns on that spending stay low for longer than the price assumes.

worth.text: The price is 25.3 times trailing earnings and 20.0 times next year's estimate. It is also 10.4 times sales, against a peer median of 3.5. A discounted cash flow model values a business on its future cash, discounted back to today. Starting from today's 60.0B of free cash flow, it gives 180.1 to 286.88 per share, with a base of 217.44. To justify the current price, free cash flow would have to start growing at about 39.7% a year. Even 30% starting growth only gets to 341.8. Against its own past, the picture is different. Using its usual 5-year price-to-sales range, the stock is worth 475.73 to 592.92, with a middle of 535.43. Today's price-to-sales sits at the 33rd percentile of its own 5-year history. The two methods are more than 2x apart, and one assumption explains the gap. The cash-flow model takes today's depressed cash flow as the starting point. The history method assumes investors keep paying what they have paid before. Two of three measures lean expensive. Because the business is improving, the fair range uses the own-history numbers, and the price now sits near the bottom of that range.
worth.key_assumption: The spending that cut free cash flow from 78.0B to 60.0B turns back into cash, so next-year earnings (estimate 24.2) are the right basis for value, not today's cash flow.
